newsitem.title: CANADA: B.C. forestry firms begin union talks.
newsitem.headline: B.C. forestry firms begin union talks.

text.p: British Columbia's forest companies met with union representatives on Tuesday after wildcat strikers returned to work.

The chief negotiator for the forest companies called off negotiations just hours before they were scheduled to begin on Monday, citing the illegal strike by about 1,500 loggers in the Fraser Valley, a prime logging region northeast of Vancouver.
The loggers, who were concerned that an increase in heli-logging would cost them their jobs, were ordered back to work today by their union, said the companies' chief negotiator Keith Bennett.
Officials from the IWA-Canada union, which represents 29,000 lumber workers, were not immediately available for comment.
Union representatives met with Forest Industrial Relations, which represents about 65 companies on the British Columbia coast, for a short technical session to outline each group's opening position.
Bennett said he expected the initial session would be brief. The next negotiating session could be scheduled for about two weeks from Tuesday, he said.
"I expect there will be a bit of a hiatus," Bennett said.

Unions representing workers in the lumber and paper sectors are demanding wage increases and greater job security. The British Columbia forest industry, however, is expected to lose C$450 million this year after losses of C$250 million in 1996.
The IWA-Canada union will also meet with the bargaining agents for companies in the interior of the province, but the coastal contract acts as the benchmark for all regions.
British Columbia is a major exporter of lumber to the United States and Japan. The province sells about 9.5 billion board feet of lumber to the United States, or about 20 percent of the market there.
